title: Trophic cascade

definition.text: A chain of indirect effects through a food web that follows when one feeding level is suppressed, which can reshape a whole ecosystem.

facts.text: In a top-down cascade, predators cut prey numbers or change prey behaviour, freeing the level below; removing top predators lets consumers overrun producers.
Removing fish-eating fish from a lake can turn the water from clear to green as phytoplankton flourish.
Where sea otters were hunted out, sea urchins increased and kelp declined.
Overfishing of Atlantic cod in the Baltic Sea let its prey, sprat, take over, which then reduced the copepods sprat eat.
Aldo Leopold first described the mechanism after seeing deer overgraze mountains once wolves were exterminated.
Yellowstone's wolf reintroduction is popularly cited as a cascade, but the ecosystem is too complex and open to be a straightforward example.
That cascades exist is not controversial, but how widespread they are has long been debated.

contested_note: Ecologists agree trophic cascades exist but have long debated how widespread they are.

title: Terrestrial trophic cascades

definition.text: The debate over whether trophic cascades on land are as strong as those in lakes, streams and seas.

facts.text: The earliest documented cascades were all aquatic, leading to speculation that cascades are mainly an aquatic phenomenon.
A 2002 meta-analysis found cascades generally weaker on land, with smaller changes in plant biomass.
A 2009 study found many tree species were heavily affected by the loss of an apex predator.
Critics note real food webs blur trophic levels through omnivory, diet changes with growth and outside resource inputs.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether land ecosystems show cascades as strong as aquatic ones.

definition.text: The movement of energy through the living things of an ecosystem.

facts.text: Producers turn sunlight into stored chemical energy as glucose through photosynthesis; respiration reverses this, releasing energy.
Organisms are organized into producers and consumers in food chains, and those chains into trophic pyramids.
Secondary production by herbivores and decomposers depends on primary productivity.
Primary producers fix carbon at similar rates across ecosystems, but how energy moves to higher levels differs.
Energy flow depends on primary productivity together with temperature, water and light.

title: Free-market environmentalism

definition.text: The view that free markets, property rights and lawsuits for harm are the best way to protect the environment and conserve resources.

facts.text: Its advocates argue that clear, protected property rights let parties negotiate better environmental outcomes and sue to stop harm.
They blame environmental problems on laws that obscure property rights and on transaction costs too high for bargaining.
Critics say it cannot handle collective problems, since resources such as water are hard to privatize and pollution is hard to trace.

contested_note: Critics argue market tools cannot handle collective environmental problems, while proponents see property rights as the best remedy.
